 Learner Tien, the American lefty who wins without a big serve
 Photo: Hameltion / CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons — Wikimedia Commons 
 By 
 Penelope H. Fritz 
 5 min read 
 Add us on Google 
 Learner Tien Photo: Hameltion / CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Born December 2, 2005
 Irvine 
 Occupation Tennis Player 
 Awards Next Gen ATP Finals champion · Moselle Open champion · Geneva Open champion · Australian Open boys' doubles champion 
 Learner Tien plays tennis as if the last decade of the men’s game had not happened. The sport has been rebuilt around the first strike, the serve that ends a point before it begins and the forehand that finishes the next ball. Tien, a left-hander from southern California, does most of his damage after that phase is over. He returns deep, runs down balls that were meant to be winners, sends the ball long and high to the backhand corner and waits for the other man to lose patience. It keeps working against people who were supposed to overpower him: Daniil Medvedev three times, Alexander Zverev once, Ben Shelton twice. What his career is asking now is whether that game can carry him past the players he upsets and into the small group that wins the biggest titles, with a serve that rarely frightens anyone.
 His first name tells you something about the house he grew up in. His mother, Huyen, taught mathematics; his father, Khuong, is a real-estate lawyer, and his sister is called Justice. Both parents are Hoa, ethnic Chinese from Vietnam, who left the south of the country after the war by different routes, he by plane and she by boat. In a Tennis Channel documentary Huyen described a crossing of ten days and the people she saw die on the way. The couple met through tennis in Irvine, and their son found the game on the public courts there, hanging around while his father played in a men’s league.
 Tien was born in Irvine on December 2, 2005, and won his first tournament, at the Racquet Club of Irvine, when he was five. His mother homeschooled him. He finished high school at 16 and that summer won the USTA Boys 18s national championship in Kalamazoo, which earned him a wildcard into the 2022 US Open; no one younger had played the men’s main draw there since Donald Young in 2005. Miomir Kecmanović beat him in four sets. In 2023 he reached the boys’ singles final at both the Australian Open and the US Open, losing the first to Alexander Blockx and the second to João Fonseca, and won the Australian Open boys’ doubles with Cooper Williams. After a semester at the University of Southern California he turned professional.
 The climb ran through the lower tiers. In the summer of 2024 he won 28 matches in a row on the ITF and Challenger circuits, a streak that included his first Challenger title, at Cranbrook in Michigan. That autumn he added titles in Las Vegas and Fairfield, where he beat Bernard Tomic in 39 minutes, the shortest final in Challenger history, and as a qualifier ranked 231st he reached the quarter-finals of the ATP event in Winston-Salem. In December he reached the final of the Next Gen ATP Finals in Saudi Arabia and lost it to Fonseca, again.
 Melbourne changed the scale in January 2025. Through qualifying, he beat Medvedev, the fifth seed, in a second-round match that lasted four hours and 50 minutes, ended after three in the morning and was settled by a fifth-set tiebreak to ten points. He reached the fourth round, the second-youngest American man to get that far at the Australian Open in the Open Era, after Pete Sampras. A month later, in Acapulco, he beat Zverev, then world No. 2, 6-3 6-4. In July he started working with Michael Chang, the 1989 French Open champion, who had made his name as a coach with Kei Nishikori. By the autumn the work showed. In Beijing he beat Lorenzo Musetti and then Medvedev, who retired in the third set, before Jannik Sinner took the final 6-2 6-2. In Metz he won his first ATP title, edging Cameron Norrie in a third-set tiebreak to become the first American teenager to win a tour title since Andy Roddick in 2002. In December he won the Next Gen ATP Finals, beating Blockx, the player who had beaten him in the Australian Open junior final.
 In January 2026 he returned to Melbourne as a seed and, in the fourth round, met Medvedev again and beat him in straight sets, handing the Russian the first 6-0 set he had ever lost at a major, to reach his first Grand Slam quarter-final, where Zverev stopped him. He reached the quarter-finals at Indian Wells, beating Shelton before losing to Sinner, then won his first clay title at the Geneva Open in May, beating Alexander Bublik in the semi-final and Mariano Navone in the final, the youngest champion there since Marc Rosset in 1989. In August he reached a career-high No. 12 and, in Montreal, his first Masters semi-final.
 The upsets are the part of the story that travels, and they hide the harder part. Against the top ten his record is close to even, and the defeats follow a pattern: Sinner beat him in the Beijing final and again at Indian Wells, Zverev stopped him in Melbourne, and in the Montreal semi-final Shelton, whom he had beaten twice, won 6-2 6-3. Two of his wins in that Beijing run came against opponents who retired. Outside Melbourne, he has never gone past the fourth round of a major, and Wimbledon, where the serve is worth most, has produced two second-round exits. The counterpuncher label flatters a player who can outlast almost anyone, but it also describes one whose best wins tend to be the longest ones, and long matches are a tax that compounds over two weeks of a major.
 The US Open showed both sides. He beat Gaël Monfils in the second round of the Frenchman’s farewell tournament, then came back from two sets to one down against Jakub Menšík in three hours and 24 minutes to reach the fourth round. There he led Karen Khachanov by two sets to one and lost in five. In September he made his Laver Cup debut for Andre Agassi’s Team World at the O2 in London, beat Flavio Cobolli and lost to Zverev on the final day as Team Europe won 13-5. The Asian swing was thinner: a first-round defeat to Hubert Hurkacz in Beijing and a third-round loss to Casper Ruud in Shanghai.
 Ranked 18th in the world, he opened the Erste Bank Open in Vienna on Monday by beating Luca Van Assche 6-3 6-1, and Alex de Minaur is next. He turns 21 on December 2, a month before the Australian Open, the tournament where his patience has paid best and where, in January, he will try to prove that a player who wins the long way can also win the big one.
